thread.title: Requiem Of A GE Bull

author: SeekingAlpha
title: Requiem Of A GE Bull
text:
Shutterstock photo By Brian Gilmartin, CFA : While 2017 was a good year for client accounts, with Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Schwab ( SCHW ) being the vast majority of clients' top 2 weightings in their separate accounts for the past several years, the fact is General Electric ( GE ) also had a "top 10" position in client accounts in 2017.
The allure of the stock was well understood:
1) As a well-diversified industrial with business lines in Aerospace/Defense, Energy, Health Care, and the old stalwart GE Capital, it was easy to hang on to the stock post-2008 given the damage at that time to the financial sector, and the hope for a US and global economic and industrial recovery.
2) GE's management was always thought to be "best-in-class" with the development of "6 Sigma" and the so-called black belt in management training. GE's philosophy was to always have the #1 or #2 positions in whatever market segment they chose to operate in and would be brutally Darwinian about retaining key employees and managers. Whether real or Street lore, there was a rumor that GE would cull the bottom 10% of employees and managers yearly, thereby reinforcing the "up-or-out" philosophy.
3) Looking at its valuation post-2008, GE's valuation was never outlandish or out of whack with either the other industrials or with the S&P 500 as a whole. Between 2012 and 2016 it was thought that GE could generate $3 per share in cash from operations and $1.50-$1.75 in free cash flow per share, and according to the spreadsheet I kept on GE, with full P/L, balance sheet, statement of cash flows and earnings and revenue estimates. As late as 2015 GE's operating cash flow per share ((OCFPS)) was $2.95-$2.97 per share.
At one point in mid-2016, GE Industrial alone generated $3.50 in OCFPS according to the published financials.
And therein lies the rub: listening to some of the comments about the auditors and the GE financials today, these numbers investors were looking at could have been "Enron" or "Tyco-like" or, to Quote: a line from the movie Gladiator, "a pleasant fiction".
Again, that is subject to debate, and it will be played out in the courts for years.
The writedown this past week and the increase in the insurance reserve to 3(x) to 5(x) what was expected from the insurance business was tremendous shock to the Street (not to mention the mention on the conference call of a "capital raise") and I wound up selling the remaining last position of GE held for clients.
4) With GE, with one stock, you could buy a big chunk of the S&P 500 in terms of energy, health care, aerospace/defense and of course GE Capital. Using the current market cap weights of the various sectors, these sectors comprise about between 38% and (maybe) 43% of the S&P 500, given that the financial health care sectors comprise 30% of the S&P 500 by themselves.
The beginning of doubt around GE To be frank with readers, it was always easy to own GE for clients, much the same way that it is easy today to own Apple ( AAPL ), any of the big-branded financials, a name like Intel ( INTC ), etc. Clients often hear these names and associate the name of the company with stability, dependability, brand power, etc.
The doubts around GE began to creep in this year when the rest of the industrial complex performed quite well for most of the calendar year, but from almost the first day of 2017, GE began declining and didn't really stop all year.
That is always one test for readers: whenever you have a position in a stock, monitor how it trades or performs relative to its peer group or a similar ETF. if your stock and the sector are diverging, sit up and take notice.
The other test is the S&P 500 had a good year in 2017, up 21.5%, and the index progressed in a pretty linear fashion all year. If one of your investments diverges from your benchmark, take notice of that action, too.
One other aspect too that puzzled me as GE exited the Great Recession and the Financial Crisis was that - unlike other industrial conglomerates - Jeff Immelt seem frozen with the current business lines. He seemed unwilling or incapable to reshuffle the business portfolio as is needed with these companies.
I do a lot of fundamental homework on the companies clients own - companies like GE, or United Technologies ( UTX ) or Honeywell (HON) or 3M (MMM). And one thing I've noticed over the years is that these companies' business segments, or at least the 10-Q disclosures, are always changing as the companies add and divest either product or business lines.
GE's business lines never changed much after the early 2000s. After 9/11 and the Financial Crisis, Jeff Immelt seemed like a deer in the headlights - he seemed frozen and unsure of what to do next. And as Jim Cramer has talked about quite a bit on CNBC, Jeff wound up adding to energy (Baker Hughes (BHGE)) at the high price for crude and selling substantial GE Capital assets near the low bid for financial assets.
The GE eulogy When John Flannery gave the GE conference call after Q3 '17 earnings on October 20th, 2017, I thought John was the real deal. His analysis and summary of GE Power, which John detailed from the macro and the micro level, was a thing of beauty. I thought it would be the stuff of business-school case study legend for years to come.
His assessment of the GE business segments, as he went through every segment and detailed the strengths and weaknesses of each business line and what he thought the immediate future held, was classic "competitive strategy" type analysis. My first thought was, "John is a big change from Jeff Immelt".
But most important, John Flannery didn't seem like the guy who would stand around and let the slide continue. He indicated he would be taking action, and he later did, announcing 12,000 layoffs in the GE Power division alone.
But here is the thing: GE's stock kept falling.
I have a general rule about individual equities: a stock will typically be sold from client accounts when its trades below $20 or, if bought in the high single digits or low double digits, if it trades below $5 per share.
Summary/conclusion: It was truly difficult to watch GE disintegrate slowly as it did this year. One of the great iconic American companies is being both presumably dismantled and possibly even dissolved in the next 12 to 24 months.
While the auditors have probably yet to attract the attention they should, the disclosure this week that GE might have to do a "capital raise" this week, and issue equity, is reminiscent of Citigroup (C) and AIG (AIG) after the Financial Crisis. A capital raise usually screams "dilution" to common shareholders, although with an A+ credit rating for GE corporate maybe the company can raise some debt along with equity to stop the bleeding.
John Flannery seems to be discovering more underlying issues as he looks to shore up the problems he was aware of coming into the job.
Think of the GE retirees who owned the stock in taxable accounts and maybe were afraid to sell or tax the capital gain earlier this year and now are sitting with a 40% or 50% decline in their primary retirement asset and still in shock because of it.
